description: QUASAR SELJUK: 6 visionary BİLSEM students united for the NASA Space Apps Challenge! Inspired by cosmic energy and scientific heritage, we are a multidisciplinary think-tank. Combining Software and Space Sciences with the creativity of Gaming & Design, the strategic power of Chess, and the harmony of Music we transform raw NASA data into innovative tech solutions. Driven by art and code, our crew is ready for launch!
summary:
Kuasar Crew Health is a daily self-check tool that lets astronauts assess their own health without waiting for the ground. The crew member logs 25 readings a day, such as blood pressure, blood oxygen, eye ultrasound, radiation dose, sleep, mood and symptoms. The app compares each value with clinical reference ranges and with the astronaut's own usual value, then shows a 0–100 health score, a body map of where a problem is, and the three most important next steps.

This matters because on long missions the flight surgeon is not always a call away: a signal from Mars can take 20 minutes to reach Earth. The app reads readings together, so 15 rules and 14 emergency checks can recognise problems such as cabin pressure loss and give the first action at once. It runs as one HTML file in any browser, with no installation and no internet, and keeps all data on the device.
details:
What it does. Kuasar Crew Health turns a short daily check-in into a clear answer to three questions: how am I, what is wrong, and what should I do now. It is built for crew members on the ISS, a Moon or Mars base, or in Mars transit, and adjusts signal delay and radiation expectations to the chosen environment.

How it works.

1. Daily check-in. 25 readings grouped into cards, with units inside the fields and live in-range feedback. A day bar shows which mission day is being logged.

2. Personal baseline. Each reading is compared with its clinical range and with the astronaut's own usual value learned from earlier days. A combined statistical check flags several readings drifting together.

3. Rules and emergency checks. 15 explainable rules and 14 emergency checks (cabin pressure loss, fire, CO₂ build-up, solar particle event, heart problems, decompression sickness and more) point to likely causes. Causes are tested against the data and shown as supported or ruled out.

4. Action. A 0–100 health score with grades A–E, the three most useful next steps, a one-tap report to the crew medical officer and flight surgeon (simulated), and daily, weekly or monthly PDF reports.

Other features. Body map, simulated live telemetry with sensor alerts, a performance early warning with a reaction-time test, water and nutrition tracking against NASA targets, a digestion screen based on the Bristol stool scale, a morale survey, a medical kit tracker, and a simulation mode that tests every emergency without touching real data. The whole interface switches between English and Turkish.

Benefits. Faster self-assessment when communication is delayed, fewer missed warning signs because readings are read together, and short reports that save the flight surgeon time.

Tools. HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript in a single file with no external libraries; a built-in PDF writer with an embedded DejaVu Sans font; Node.js for automated tests (3,943 checks) and Playwright with Chromium for interface checks. Hosted on GitHub and GitHub Pages. Source code: https://github.com/Dragnar1250/crew-health
